questions.stem: Consider the rectangle \(ABCD\) shown, where \(P\) and \(Q\) are the midpoints of \(AD\) and \(BC\) respectively. Prove, with full geometric reasoning, that \(PQ\) bisects \(BD\).
questions.hint: Show that \(APQB\) (or \(DPQC\)) is a parallelogram, and use the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
questions.solution: Since \(AP\parallel BQ\) and \(AP=BQ\) (both are half of the equal, parallel sides \(AD\) and \(BC\)), \(APQB\) is a parallelogram. Its diagonals \(PQ\) is not itself a diagonal of \(APQB\) though — instead, consider that \(PQ\) and \(BD\) are the two diagonals of parallelogram \(PBQD\)... the cleanest approach: since \(PBQD\) has \(PD\parallel BQ\) and \(PD=BQ\) (each equal to half of \(AD=BC\)), \(PBQD\) is a parallelogram, so its diagonals \(PQ\) and \(BD\) bisect each other.

steps.explain: Since \(ABCD\) is a rectangle, \(AD\parallel BC\) and \(AD=BC\).
\(P\) is the midpoint of \(AD\), so \(PD=\dfrac12AD\). \(Q\) is the midpoint of \(BC\), so \(BQ=\dfrac12BC\). Since \(AD=BC\), it follows that \(PD=BQ\).
Also, \(PD\) lies along \(AD\) and \(BQ\) lies along \(BC\), and since \(AD\parallel BC\), we have \(PD\parallel BQ\).
A quadrilateral with one pair of opposite sides both equal AND parallel is a parallelogram. So \(PBQD\) is a parallelogram.
steps.work: \(\therefore PBQD\) is a parallelogram (since \(PD\parallel BQ\) and \(PD=BQ\))

steps.explain: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. The diagonals of \(PBQD\) are \(PQ\) and \(DB\).

questions.stem: Name a special quadrilateral which is not necessarily a trapezium.
questions.hint: A trapezium has at least one pair of parallel sides. Think of a special quadrilateral that does not need to have any parallel sides.

steps.work: \text{A trapezium is a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel sides.}

steps.explain: Analyze the given options to see which one does not guarantee parallel sides.
steps.work: \text{Parallelograms, rectangles, and rhombuses all have two pairs of parallel sides, meaning they are always trapeziums.}

steps.explain: Consider the properties of a kite.
steps.work: \text{A kite has two pairs of adjacent equal sides, but it generally has no parallel sides.}

steps.explain: Conclude which quadrilateral fits the criteria.
steps.work: \text{Therefore, a kite is not necessarily a trapezium.}

questions.stem: Consider the quadrilateral \(ABCD\), in which \(AB\parallel PQ\parallel DC\), \(AP=PD\) and \(BQ=QC\). Intervals \(AB\), \(PQ\) and \(DC\) are related by \(AB=2x-7\), \(PQ=x+1\) and \(DC=x-3\), for some value \(x\). Prove that \(x=12\).
questions.hint: Since \(P\) and \(Q\) are midpoints of \(AD\) and \(BC\), \(PQ\) is the midsegment of trapezium \(ABCD\), so \(PQ\) equals the average of the two parallel sides \(AB\) and \(DC\).
questions.solution: By the midsegment (trapezium) theorem, \(PQ=\dfrac12(AB+DC)\). Substituting the given expressions and solving gives \(x=12\).
